1.sense: One word stands alone as an entire verse, a definite noun with no sentence built around it. Al-Haqqah comes from the root of haqq, what is true and what is owed, so the name holds both senses at once: the thing that must come, and the thing that will prove true. It is named before anything at all is said about it.

notes.t: The root h-q-q gives haqq for truth, for a right, and for a debt that falls due. The feminine form here names an event the way one names a claim that is certain to be collected.
Al-Qari'ah opens with the same three steps, the name alone, then the question, then the widening of the question, and it names the same day by a different action.

The surah gives the day three names in its first fifteen verses: al-Haqqah, al-Qari'ah in verse four, al-Waqi'ah in verse fifteen. Each is a participle, so each names the day by what it does rather than when it is.

links.why: the same opening move under a different name for the day
the day named by its falling, and the denial of that fall ruled out

2.sense: A question that repeats the name instead of answering it. Ma here is not seeking information but enlarging, and the Arabic puts the noun as subject with the interrogative as its predicate, so the sentence closes back on itself. The effect is that the thing is too large for the word that names it.

notes.t: The construction repeats a noun already given rather than replacing it with a pronoun, which is a device of magnification in Arabic rather than of clarification.
The same frame is used of the two companies on that day, the noun stated and then questioned in place of a description.

links.why: the identical second step in the parallel surah

3.sense: The third step widens the gap rather than closing it. Adraka is a verb of being brought to knowledge, so what is asked is whether anything in the listener's own experience could supply the meaning. The answer, when it comes in the next verse, is not a definition but a history.

notes.t: The Qur'an keeps two forms of this question apart. Where it says ma adraka, an answer follows; where it says ma yudrika, the answer is withheld and the matter is left with Allah.
Ma adraka introduces Saqar, the Night of Decree and the Day of Judgement, and in each case the verse or verses after it supply what was asked.
Ma yudrika is used of the hour and of the man who came seeking, and in both places nothing further is disclosed.

links.why: the same verse in the parallel surah, answered there by a scale rather than a history
the other form of the question, left open

4.sense: The answer to the question is a history, not a definition. Two named peoples are put in front as the ones who called the day a lie, and the day is given a fourth-verse renaming, al-Qari'ah, the thing that strikes. Thamud and 'Ad were the standing Arabian example of a people who heard the warning and stayed where they were.

notes.t: Qari'ah is from q-r-', to knock or strike. A qari'ah is a blow that lands, and the word is used in ordinary Arabic for a disaster that arrives suddenly on a house.
The Prophet ﷺ is told to warn Quraysh with a thunderbolt like the thunderbolt of 'Ad and Thamud, which is why these two peoples stand first in a Meccan argument.

links.why: the surah named for this word
'Ad of the pillars and Thamud who cut the rock in the valley

5.sense: The two peoples are now taken one at a time, each with its own instrument. Thamud went by at-taghiyah, a feminine noun from the root of tughyan, the going past of a limit. The verb is passive, so the agent is left out and only the instrument is named.

notes.t: The root t-gh-y runs through the surah. It gives taghut, tughyan, and the verb tagha used of the flood water in verse eleven. Each people in the passage is destroyed by something bearing the name of its own fault.

At-taghiyah is read as the cry that took Thamud, as the thunderbolt, and as their own overstepping, taken up by the man who hamstrung the she-camel. The word gives no noun to settle it and the disagreement is old.
notes.src: at-Tabari collects the cry and the transgression readings from the early commentators

notes.t: Thamud is elsewhere said to have denied by its taghwa, from this same root, so the transgression reading has a hold inside the Qur'an.

links.why: the cry that took the wrongdoers and left them prone in their homes
Thamud introduced with the same wa-amma frame and taken by a thunderbolt

6.sense: 'Ad went by wind. Sarsar carries both noise and cold in a doubled root that sounds like the thing it names, and 'atiyah is a participle of overstepping, the same charge laid against Thamud in the verse before. The instrument is ordinary air, given no limit.

notes.t: Sarsar is built by reduplication, the syllable repeated, which Arabic uses for continuous noise. The word carries the shriek of the wind and its bitterness together.
The wind sent on 'Ad is named with this same adjective, sent across days called ill-omened.
The same wind again, sent on a day of continuing misfortune, in the surah that supplies the palm-trunk image of the next verse.

links.why: the barren wind that left nothing it passed over
the cloud they took for rain coming down their valleys

7.sense: The wind is given a term: seven nights and eight days running, husuman, one after another with nothing between. Then the scene left behind, bodies laid out where they had been standing, compared to the stumps of palms. A'jaz are the lower ends of trunks, so what is left is not a tree but the base of one, and khawiyah says it is empty inside.

notes.t: Husum is from h-s-m, the verb for searing a wound shut with hot iron and for cutting a matter off for good. The days are consecutive and they finish the thing.
The same image is used of 'Ad in Al-Qamar, the people torn out as though they were the stumps of uprooted palms. There the trunks are pulled up, here they are hollow.
Sar'a is the plural of sari', one thrown down, and it is the word for a wrestler's fall. It describes position rather than cause: they are where they were dropped.

links.why: the parallel simile, uprooted rather than hollow
the days of the wind counted as ill-omened days

8.sense: A question put to whoever is looking now. Baqiyah is a feminine participle used as a noun, and it can carry a surviving person, a surviving trace, or a thing that lasts. Nothing decides between the three, so the question sweeps all of them.

notes.t: The question is rhetorical in form but concrete in address. Quraysh knew the sites and passed them on the trade roads, so the looking asked for was literal.
Of 'Ad it is said that nothing could be seen of them afterward but their dwellings, which is the answer this question expects.
The ruins of 'Ad and Thamud are elsewhere said to have been made plain to the very people being addressed here.

links.why: the wind that destroyed everything by its Lord's command

9.sense: The list widens past Arabia. Pharaoh, the peoples before him, and al-mu'tafikat, the towns that were turned over, all arrive bringing the same thing. Ja'a bi is to come carrying something, so al-khati'ah, the offence, is treated as freight rather than as a record.

notes.t: Mu'tafikat is from '-f-k, the root of ifk, a lie. An ifk is a statement turned away from what is so, and these towns were turned in the ground the way speech is turned from the truth.
The overturned town is named in An-Najm as something He brought down, and elsewhere the town of Lut is described as having its top made its bottom.
Al-khati'ah is a deliberate fault, not an error. The word returns at the close of the punishment passage in verse thirty-seven, so the same root frames what lies between.

links.why: the town turned upside down when the command came

10.sense: One verb covers every people just named: they disobeyed the messenger their Lord sent them. Rasul is singular though the peoples are many, because each had one and the offence is identical in each case. Rabiyah is from the root behind riba, what grows past its own size, so the grip is measured against the deed and then exceeds it.

notes.t: The root r-b-w means to swell or mount up. Riba is the increase added to a loan, and rabwah is a rise in the ground. The seizing is described by its growth, not by its method.
The same construction is used of Pharaoh alone, disobeying the messenger and seized with a crushing grip.
The seizing of towns that are in the wrong is described as His way, and as painful and severe.

links.why: the identical verb pair, applied to Pharaoh by himself

11.sense: The flood sits in the middle of the destructions and comes out differently. The verb used of the water, tagha, is the one behind at-taghiyah in verse five, so the water oversteps its bound as the peoples overstepped theirs. And the address changes to a second person plural: those carried are the listeners' own line, which makes the survivors the point of the sentence.

notes.t: Al-jariyah is a feminine active participle, the one that runs, used of ships. The plural of it, al-jawari, is used elsewhere of vessels standing in the sea like mountains.
Ships are named by that running participle among the signs, which is why the ark here is called by what it does rather than by the word for boat.
The ark is elsewhere described by its planks and its nails, and the carrying of the human line in a laden vessel is given as a sign.

links.why: the ark described by its timber
the ark boarded in the name of Allah, its running and its mooring

12.sense: The purpose of the rescue is stated outright: it is left standing as a reminder. Wa'a is the verb for a vessel holding what is poured into it, and the noun wi'a' is a container, so a retaining ear is one that keeps rather than one that merely hears. The root is repeated in verb and adjective, which puts the weight on holding rather than on listening.

notes.t: From the same root comes wi'a', a sack or vessel, used in the Qur'an of the bags searched in Yusuf's story. The ear is being described as a container with a capacity.
The ark and those aboard it are elsewhere said to have been made a sign for all the worlds, which is this verse's tadhkirah stated as a sign.
Tadhkirah returns at verse forty-eight, said there of the Qur'an itself. A rescued vessel and a recited book are given the same noun at the two ends of the surah.

links.why: left as a sign, followed by a question about who will remember

13.sense: The surah leaves history and moves to the day itself. The verb is passive and the blower is not named, and the blast is counted: one. From here to verse eighteen each event is finished before the next begins.

notes.t: Nafkhah is a noun of a single occurrence, so the count is already inside the word before wahidah is added. The adjective is emphasis on a number the form had given.
Two blasts are counted elsewhere, one at which all in the heavens and the earth fall, and a second after which they are standing and looking on.

The commentators differ over which of the two blasts is meant here. The verse names only that it is one, and the scene that follows is read as beginning with the first blast by some and with the second by others.
notes.src: the disagreement is set out by at-Tabari and turns on whether verses 14 to 18 are one sequence or two

links.why: the two blasts distinguished
the quaking one and the one that follows it

14.sense: The earth and the mountains are picked up before they are broken, and the verb dukkata is dual, so the two are handled as one object. Dakk is the flattening of a raised thing down into level ground. Wahidah again, so the whole of it takes one stroke.

notes.t: From d-k-k comes dakka', level ground. The barrier of Dhu al-Qarnayn is said to be made dakka' when the promise comes, and the mountain before Musa is made dakkan, which fixes the sense as levelling rather than shattering.
The same pair, earth and mountains, is taken up and reduced in Al-Waqi'ah, the earth shaken and the mountains crumbled into scattered dust.

links.why: the mountains scattered and the earth left a plain with no dip or rise in it
the barrier levelled when the promise comes

15.sense: The day is given its third name. Al-Waqi'ah is built from the verb standing in front of it, so the sentence says the falling has fallen, a pairing that makes the event and its name one thing. Al-Haqqah, al-Qari'ah and al-Waqi'ah are three participles for the same day.

notes.t: Arabic pairs a verb with a noun from its own root for emphasis. Here the noun is the subject rather than an object, which leaves nothing outside the event to describe it with.
Al-Waqi'ah opens with the same verb and noun and then rules out any calling of its fall a lie.

links.why: the surah named for this word

16.sense: The roof gives. Waha is said of a rope fraying, of a wall about to go, and of a waterskin that has begun to leak, so wahiyah is not broken but no longer holding. The sky is elsewhere described as built firm and without a rift, which is what turns this adjective into an event.

notes.t: The root w-h-y describes loss of tension rather than impact. What is named is a thing that has stopped being able to hold, which is a different picture from the shattering in the verse before.
The sky in its present state is put to the eye as having no rift in it, and the eye is told to look again and find one.
It is elsewhere said to have been built with power, which is the state this verse reverses.

links.why: the same verb, the sky splitting and turning red like oiled leather
the sky giving way, opening a surah on the same day

17.sense: Al-malak is singular in form and collective in sense, so the angels stand along the rims of the sky that has just come apart. Arja' are the sides of a thing, the walls of a well or the flanks of a valley, the parts away from the middle. Then a number is given with no noun attached to it: eight, bearing the Throne above them.

notes.t: Arja' is the plural of raja, the lip or inner wall of a well. The angels are placed at the margins because the middle is where the sky has opened.
The bearers of the Throne are named elsewhere without a count, along with those around it, glorifying and asking forgiveness for the believers.
Thamaniyah is read as eight angels and as eight ranks of them. The verse supplies no counted noun after the number, so nothing inside it settles the question.
notes.src: at-Tabari records both the eight bearers and the eight ranks from the early commentators

links.why: the bearers of the Throne, uncounted
the angels ranged round the Throne on that day

18.sense: 'Urida is the verb for troops passed in review or goods laid out for inspection, so the presenting is public and in order. The second half turns one root twice: nothing hidden of you stays hidden. Khafiyah is feminine and indefinite, which in this construction reaches every single item however small.

notes.t: The surah keeps doing this: waqa'at with al-waqi'ah, dukkata with dakkah, takhfa with khafiyah. A verb and a noun from one root, so the sentence has no room for anything outside itself.
The same day is described as one on which they are out in the open and nothing of them is hidden from Allah.

links.why: presented before the Lord in ranks, arriving as they were first created

19.sense: The fa-amma that sorted Thamud from 'Ad now sorts people. Ha'um is an imperative of offering, hold this and take it, and it carries a plural ending, so the man is calling others over. The first thing he does with the record is hand it around.

notes.t: Ha'umu is a rare form, an interjection that takes verb endings. Its plural addressee shows he is speaking to a crowd rather than answering a judge.
The ha at the end of kitabiyah is the ha' as-sakt, a silent letter written to carry the pause. It runs on the rhyme through verses nineteen to twenty-nine and then stops.
The same man appears in Al-Inshiqaq, given the record in his right hand, reckoned with easily, and returning to his people glad.

links.why: the same clause, followed by an easy reckoning
each people called with its record, and those given it in the right hand reading it

20.sense: The ground for handing the record around is given in one line, and it is not a list of deeds. Zanna runs from a passing thought to settled conviction, and the context here fixes it at the strong end: he lived expecting this meeting. What is put forward as the reason is the expectation itself.

notes.t: Zann is decided by its context rather than by its form. The same verb carries guessing in one place and certainty in another, and Arabic lets both stand under the one word.
The humble are described with this exact verb and participle, those who are certain they are meeting their Lord and returning to Him.
The verb carries plain certainty again where the guilty see the Fire and know they are falling into it.

links.why: the same words used of the living, before the day

21.sense: 'Ishah is not life as a span but life as it is lived, the manner of it. Radiyah is an active participle, so the Arabic says a contented living rather than a contenting one, giving the satisfaction to the life instead of to the man. The attribute is moved from its owner onto the thing he holds.

notes.t: Arabic will hand an active participle to the thing rather than the person, so a day can be described as fasting and a life as pleased. English has to reverse it to make sense of it.
The identical clause closes the heavy pan of the scale in Al-Qari'ah, the surah whose opening this one shares.

links.why: the same phrase reached through the weighing of the scales

22.sense: One prepositional phrase, no verb in it. 'Aliyah is height of place and of rank together, and the word is chosen so the next verse can undercut it. A high garden would ordinarily put its fruit out of reach.

notes.t: The three verses twenty-one to twenty-three shorten as they go, four words then three then two, so the description narrows down onto the fruit.
The same phrase describes the garden of the faces that are bright on that day.

links.why: the same garden reached through faces at ease with their striving

23.sense: Qutuf are what is picked, from qatafa, to pluck fruit, so the noun already has a hand in it. Daniyah answers 'aliyah in the line before: the garden is high and the fruit is low. Nothing about the picking is described, only the distance.

notes.t: The pair 'aliyah and daniyah are opposites set two words apart, height given to the place and nearness to the produce, so neither cancels the other.
The same clusters are described elsewhere as brought low and made to submit to the hand.

links.why: the fruit of the two gardens near at hand

24.sense: Two imperatives, and the reason attached to them. Aslafa is to pay in advance, the merchant's word for money put down before goods are delivered, so the deeds are treated as a payment already made. The days are called khaliyah, emptied and finished, and what was spent in them is what is now drawn on.

notes.t: Salaf is the forward sale, payment now against delivery later. The word makes the earlier life the paying end of a transaction whose goods are being handed over in this verse.
The same command with the same relish is given in At-Tur, there with the deeds named plainly rather than as a payment.
What is sent ahead for oneself is elsewhere said to be found waiting with Allah, which is the arrangement this verse settles.

links.why: the identical imperative pair with a different reason clause

25.sense: The mirror of verse nineteen, word for word until the hand changes. The first man's sentence opens by offering the record to others; this one's opens with laytani, a wish turned inward. He does not dispute the record, he wishes it out of existence.

notes.t: Both speeches are built on one frame, amma man utiya kitabahu, and they part at a single word. Everything after that word is a consequence of the hand.
Al-Inshiqaq gives the same man with a different placement, the record handed to him behind his back.

links.why: the record given from behind
the record brought out on that day already open

26.sense: The wish extends: not to have been given the record, and not to have learned what the reckoning came to. Adri is the verb of verse three, where nothing in a listener's experience could reach al-Haqqah. The same verb is now used by a man who has reached it and wants the knowing undone.

notes.t: Dara in verse three is used of a knowledge no one can get to. Here it is used of a knowledge no one can get rid of. The surah puts the two ends of that verb at its two ends.
The guilty elsewhere cry out at a record that leaves out nothing small and nothing large, which is what makes it unwishable away.

links.why: the book that omits nothing

27.sense: The pronoun in laytaha reaches back to the death he has already died. Al-Qadiyah is from qada, to settle a matter and be done with it, so the wish is that dying had closed the account rather than opened it. It is the second wish in three verses and it asks for less than the first.

notes.t: Qada is the judge's verb, to decide and finish. Making it a feminine participle turns the deciding into a thing that could have happened and did not.
No death is tasted there after the first one, which is exactly what this wish is asking to have been otherwise.

links.why: the denier wishing he were dust
neither dying in it nor living

28.sense: Aghna 'an is to stand in place of something and make it unneeded, so the complaint is that the wealth could not be substituted for whatever is now required. The verb comes first and the possessive comes last, which leaves maliyah on the rhyme. Two things are named as having failed him, this one and the one in the next verse.

notes.t: Ghina is being free of need. The fourth form, aghna, is to make someone free of need, so the negation says the wealth could not buy him out of a single requirement.
The same verb and the same noun are used of Abu Lahab, whose wealth and earnings availed him nothing.

links.why: a day on which neither wealth nor sons are of use
his wealth not availing him when he falls

29.sense: Sultan covers both power over people and the proof a man argues with, and both senses fit a speaker holding a record he cannot dispute. Halaka is the verb used of 'Ad and Thamud in verses five and six, so the word that took whole peoples is now used of one man's standing. The rhyme that has run since the first verse ends here.

notes.t: Sultan is from salata, to have hold over. The Qur'an uses it for a ruler's grip and for an argument's force, and nothing in the verse chooses between them.
Verses one to twenty-nine rhyme in a long -iyah. Verses thirty to thirty-two break to a short -uh, and the rest of the surah runs on -in and -im. The break falls exactly where the speech is cut off.
Arriving alone, with everything that was granted left behind, is stated elsewhere as the shape of that arrival.

links.why: coming one by one, with the granted things left behind
no party to help him and no help in himself

30.sense: The speech stops in the middle of its complaint and an order is given over his head, in the plural, to keepers who are never named. Ghull is the iron collar joining the neck to the hands, and the verb makes it the first thing done. Three short commands then follow one another with nothing in between.

notes.t: The plural imperative goes to an unnamed party, so the man who has been speaking for five verses is now spoken about rather than spoken to. He gets no further line.
Collars on the necks and chains they are dragged by are described together elsewhere as the state of those who denied.

links.why: chains, collars and a blaze prepared

31.sense: The object is put in front of its verb, so the Blaze is named first and the command lands after it. Sala is the verb for holding a thing to fire until the fire takes, used of roasting meat and of warming a bow to straighten it. Al-Jahim is fire seen as a mass of heat rather than as flame.

notes.t: Fronting the object before the verb is an Arabic device for weight. The order of the words puts the Fire ahead of what is done in it.
The same noun and the same verb are put together in Al-Infitar, the wicked in a jahim and burning in it on the Day of Judgement.

links.why: the noun and the verb paired again

32.sense: Salaka is to pass a thing through a narrow way, the verb for threading a cord through an opening. The chain is measured before the command is given, so the length is what the ear holds first. Dhira' is the forearm, a unit taken from the body.

notes.t: The measure comes before the imperative, which reverses the ordinary order and leaves the number standing alone in the middle of the verse.
The same verb is used in Al-Muddaththir as a question put to the guilty, what threaded you into Saqar, and the answer given there is the pair of charges this surah gives in the next two verses.

Seventy cubits is taken as a definite measure by some of the early commentators, who then differ over whose cubit is meant, and as a figure for great length by others. The disagreement is old and nothing in the verse resolves it.
notes.src: at-Tabari collects the differing reports on the measure

links.why: the same verb, asked rather than commanded
the guilty coupled together in fetters

33.sense: The charge comes after the sentence rather than before it. Kana with the imperfect makes it a standing habit and not one refusal: this was how he lived. The name chosen is al-'Azim, the Immense, which is the name the surah closes on nineteen verses later.

notes.t: Kana followed by an imperfect verb describes continuous past practice. The construction moves the charge from an act to a way of going on.
Al-Muddaththir gives the same two counts in the same order, and there the guilty state them against themselves: they were not among those who prayed, and they did not feed the destitute.

links.why: the two counts spoken by the condemned themselves

34.sense: The second count is not a failure to feed but a failure to press others to. Hadda is to urge and to spur, so what is missing is the pushing of a household or a town toward it. Miskin is from sukun, stillness, the one whom need has brought to a standstill.

notes.t: The charge is social rather than private. A man might feed no one because he has nothing, but urging costs nothing and is what the verb asks for.
Al-Ma'un has this clause word for word, and there it is attached to denying the reckoning, which is the same joining of the two counts made here.
Al-Fajr uses the same root in a reciprocal form, not urging one another toward feeding the destitute.

links.why: the identical clause under a different heading

35.sense: Two adverbs are stacked, al-yawma and hahuna, today and in this place, which narrows the denial to one setting rather than making a statement about friendship in general. Hamim is a relative or friend near enough to feel the heat of another's trouble. The two verses that follow take away company and food in that order, answering the two counts just laid.

notes.t: Hamim is from h-m-m, heat. The same word names scalding water elsewhere in the Qur'an, so one root gives both the friend who is close and the water that is poured.
The guilty elsewhere find no intercessors and no devoted friend, the same word in the same position.

links.why: no close friend asking after a close friend
the other sense of the word, the scalding poured over the head

36.sense: Ghislin occurs once in the Qur'an and nowhere else in it. Its form is built on ghasl, washing, which is what the reading given by most of the early commentators rests on: what runs off the bodies of the people of the Fire. The pairing with the charge is exact, since the man would not urge food for the destitute and food is what is now withheld.

notes.t: Ghislin is read as the discharge washed from the people of the Fire and, by others, as the name of a thing in Hell rather than a description of it. The word appears only here, so nothing inside the Qur'an settles the sense.
notes.src: at-Tabari carries the discharge reading from the early commentators and notes the others

notes.t: Al-Ghashiyah uses the same sentence frame with a different substance, no food for them but from dari'.
The Qur'an names more than one such food in more than one place, dari', zaqqum, and this. No single one is given as the whole account.

links.why: the same frame, a different substance
the tree of zaqqum as the food of the sinful

37.sense: Arabic keeps khati' and mukhti' apart: the first does wrong knowing it, the second gets a thing wrong by mistake. The plural chosen here is the first. Al-khati'ah in verse nine named what Pharaoh and the overturned towns brought with them, so the root that opened the passage closes it.

notes.t: The distinction is carried in the form. Yusuf's brothers use this very plural of themselves when they confess, because what they did was done on purpose.
The other form is the one used in the prayer asking not to be held to account for forgetting or erring, which is where the line between the two words is drawn.
Yusuf's brothers name themselves with this plural when they ask their father to seek forgiveness for them.

links.why: a forelock that is lying and offending, the two adjectives together

38.sense: The subject turns from the Day to the Qur'an itself, and an oath opens the new section. Fala uqsimu is read two ways: as a swearing with la added for weight, and as a refusal saying the matter needs no oath at all. What is sworn on is everything visible, and then in the next verse everything that is not.

notes.t: The la in fala uqsimu is taken as an added particle strengthening the oath and as a real negation answering something the deniers had said. Both readings are old and neither is decided by the words alone.
notes.src: at-Tabari and the grammarians set out both readings

notes.t: Al-Waqi'ah opens an oath with the same words and then calls the oath itself immense, if they only knew it.

links.why: the same oath formula, sworn on the stars that withdraw

39.sense: The second half of the oath takes in the rest. Between them the two clauses leave nothing out, since a thing is either seen or unseen, and the oath is sworn on the whole of it. The pair also sets up the division the argument that follows turns on, since what is at issue is a message with an unseen source.

notes.t: Naming two opposites to mean the totality between them is a standard Arabic device. Here the totality is creation, described from the point of view of the eye rather than of the thing.
The same pairing is used as a divine title, the Knower of the unseen and the seen, so the two halves of this oath are the two halves of what He knows.

links.why: the messenger not withholding what comes from the unseen

40.sense: The thing sworn to. Qawl rasul is the speech of one sent, and a messenger's word is by definition carried rather than composed, so the genitive itself answers the charge that is coming. Karim covers nobility of origin and generosity of hand together.

notes.t: The messenger here is read as the Prophet ﷺ, since the next two verses answer charges made against him by name, and as Jibril, since the identical clause in At-Takwir is followed by the description of an angel strong and established with the Owner of the Throne. Both readings are old.
notes.src: at-Tabari reports both; the parallel clause is 81:19-20

notes.t: The identical sentence stands in At-Takwir, where what follows it describes the one who brought it rather than the one who recited it.
The same adjective is given to the Qur'an itself in Al-Waqi'ah, so karim attaches in the Qur'an to both the message and its carrier.

links.why: the same clause, followed by an angel obeyed and trusted

41.sense: The first charge answered. Calling him a poet was a way of filing the Qur'an inside a known category, since Arabia knew poets and knew exactly what a poet's word sounded like. Qalilan ma tu'minun is a construction of near-negation, how little belief there is rather than a measured amount of it.

notes.t: Qalilan ma with an added ma is emphasis, not quantity. Arabic uses the phrase where English would say hardly at all.
Poetry was not taught to him and does not suit him, which is stated flatly in Ya-Sin as the answer to this same charge.

A long report carried in the Musnad has 'Umar say that before his Islam he stood behind the Prophet ﷺ in the mosque and heard him reciting this surah, thought first that he was hearing a poet and then a soothsayer, and heard each thought answered by the verse that came next. The chain of the report is discussed.
notes.src: Ahmad, in the Musnad, from Ibn 'Abbas relating 'Umar's own account

links.why: the charge quoted in their own words, waiting for time to do away with him

42.sense: The second charge. A kahin was a diviner dealing in short rhymed prose and claiming an unseen informant, which made him the nearest thing in Arabian life to what was being heard. The two rebuttals close on different verbs: the poet charge ends with believing, the soothsayer charge with remembering.

notes.t: The diviners used saj', rhymed cadenced prose without metre. It is the formal resemblance, not the content, that made the charge available.
At-Tur sets both charges aside in a single line, telling him he is by his Lord's favour neither a soothsayer nor possessed.

links.why: the two charges dismissed together
the charge in their mouths, a possessed poet

43.sense: After two denials, the positive statement. Tanzil is a verbal noun for the act of bringing down, so putting it in the predicate identifies the Qur'an with its own descent rather than describing it from outside. The source is named by a title that covers everything the oath two verses back was sworn on.

notes.t: The doubled middle radical in tanzil carries a sending down in stages, as against inzal for a single act. The form matches a recitation that arrived over years.
The identical line stands in Al-Waqi'ah, the surah this one also shares its last two verses with.

links.why: the same claim in the other form of the noun, at the close of Ash-Shu'ara

44.sense: A condition whose answer runs across the next two verses. Taqawwala is the fifth form of qala, and the form itself carries manufacture: to work a saying up and fasten it on someone. Al-aqawil is a plural built on a plural, which makes the objects small and scattered, so even a little of it falls inside the condition.

notes.t: Form V often carries effort or pretence. Taqawwala is not saying but getting a saying made, which is precisely the accusation being ruled out.
He is told to say that altering it from himself is not his to do, and that he follows only what is revealed to him.

links.why: the pull to invent something else against Allah, and the steadying against it

45.sense: The answer to the condition begins. Akhadha bil-yamin is the grip taken on a man's right hand to hold him, the stronger hand and the one he would act with. The phrase is also read as a seizing with power, since yamin carries strength as well as side.

notes.t: Whether bil-yamin means by his right hand or with might is disputed, and the commentators give both. Yamin in the Qur'an carries the hand, the side and the strength, and the phrase alone does not choose.
notes.src: at-Tabari records the seizing of his right hand and the seizing with power

notes.t: The same phrase is used of Ibrahim striking the idols, and it carries the same ambiguity between the hand and the force there.

links.why: the heavens folded in His right hand, yamin used of power

46.sense: The watin is the great vessel out of the heart, the one whose cutting ends everything at once. Naming it instead of saying We would have killed him keeps the sentence anatomical and immediate. Thumma orders the two acts: held first, then cut.

notes.t: Watin occurs once in the Qur'an. The Arabs used it for the cord of the heart, the vein whose severing is instant, so the word carries finality rather than violence.
Inventing a lie against Allah, or claiming a revelation that was not given, is elsewhere set beside the moment of death and the angels' outstretched hands.

links.why: the false claim of revelation and what meets it

47.sense: The condition closes by removing every defender. Hajiz is one who comes between two things and keeps them apart, from the noun for a barrier. The predicate is plural while the subject ahad is singular, so the sentence looks past the one man to the whole body it is addressing.

notes.t: The plural hajizin agrees with the sense of minkum rather than with the singular ahad. Arabic allows the agreement to follow the meaning where the meaning is a group.
The same noun is used for the barrier set between the two seas, which is the only other place the word describes anything in creation.

links.why: no shelter that day from the command of Allah

48.sense: The pronoun returns to the Qur'an after three verses about the one who carries it. Tadhkirah is the word used in verse twelve of the ship left standing after the flood, so one noun covers a rescued vessel and a recited book. Muttaqun are those who keep a guard up, from wiqayah, a shield held between.

notes.t: Taqwa is from wiqayah, the placing of something between oneself and harm. The word describes a posture rather than a feeling.
Al-Muddaththir calls it a tadhkirah and then leaves the taking of it to whoever wants it, which is the qualification this verse makes with lil-muttaqin.

links.why: the same noun with the same open condition

49.sense: The address turns back to the listeners and says plainly that some among them are calling it a lie. Mukadhdhib is the participle of the verb that opened the surah's history in verse four, where Thamud and 'Ad denied. What the sentence states is that the denial is known, not that it is unexpected.

notes.t: Kadhdhabat in verse four and mukadhdhibin here put the same root at both ends of the surah, so the peoples destroyed and the listeners addressed are named by one word.
The denial is identified elsewhere as a rejection of the signs rather than a charge of lying against him personally.

links.why: what is concealed in the breast and what is shown, known alike

50.sense: The same book is a reminder to one group and a grief to the other, and the two sentences are built identically so that the difference sits only in the last word. Hasrah is the regret that comes when a thing is past recovering. It is put on them with 'ala, the preposition of a weight resting.

notes.t: The root h-s-r carries stripping bare and wearing out. A worn-out beast is hasir, and the eye that looks and looks is described with the same word, which is the exhaustion inside this regret.
The cry itself is quoted elsewhere, a soul saying alas for what it neglected toward Allah.

links.why: the same cry, raised when the hour comes on them suddenly
the sight returning worn out, the other use of the root

51.sense: Haqq al-yaqin is a genitive of intensity, the truth that certainty itself amounts to. The Qur'an names two other grades elsewhere, the knowledge of certainty and the eye of certainty. The word haqq also carries the surah back to its first word, al-Haqqah, which is built on the same root.

notes.t: The surah opens on h-q-q and closes its argument on h-q-q. What was named in verse one as the thing that must come is named in verse fifty-one as the thing that is certainly so.
The other two grades are set out in At-Takathur, the knowledge of certainty and then the eye of certainty.
The identical phrase closes Al-Waqi'ah one verse before the identical command that closes this surah.

links.why: the three grades of certainty in order
the same two closing verses in the same order

52.sense: The surah ends on a single command, and it is given to the Prophet ﷺ alone. Sabbaha is to declare a thing free of what does not belong to it, from a root of moving off and away, so tasbih puts distance between the Lord and everything just denied. Al-'Azim is the name used in verse thirty-three of the one the condemned man would not believe in.

notes.t: Tasbih is removal rather than praise. The verb clears away what is falsely attached, which is why it closes a surah that has spent fifteen verses clearing the Qur'an of what was attached to it.
The identical command closes Al-Waqi'ah, immediately after the identical statement about the truth of certainty.

Abu Hurayra reports the Prophet ﷺ saying that two phrases are light on the tongue, heavy on the scale and beloved to the Most Merciful: subhan Allahi wa bihamdih, subhan Allahi al-'Azim. The second of them is this verse's divine name.
notes.src: Bukhari, the closing hadith of the Sahih and also in the Book of Invocations, from Abu Hurayra; Muslim carries it as well

links.why: the same command opening a surah rather than closing one
